From the first stethoscope, more than two centuries ago, to the brief chirp of gravitational waves, sound runs through the history of science. This feature visits four Stanford labs that use the whole acoustic spectrum, ultrasound included, to push medicine forward.

Bioengineer Manu Prakash built Abuzz, a “Shazam for insects” that identifies mosquito species from the wingbeat hum recorded on almost any phone, even a basic one. Pooled recordings could map species and the diseases they carry, such as Zika, malaria and dengue, as a global early-warning system, helping communities clear breeding sites and target releases of genetically modified mosquitoes. The team is also testing it on sick and healthy honeybees. Cardiologist Sean Wu and Utkan Demirci, a radiology professor and acoustic bioengineer, use Faraday waves to pack heart cells into triangles, hexagons, circles, lines and even stick figures; the dense tissue resembles natural heart muscle and could serve as disease models, drug screens and eventually repair patches, once it can be vascularized.

Neurologist Josef Parvizi and music professor Chris Chafe turned brain signals into sound with a headband “brain stethoscope” that lets almost anyone hear a seizure, including silent, nonconvulsive ones; the FDA approved it in May 2017. Amin Arbabian is developing an implant the size of two grains of rice that runs on ultrasound instead of batteries or wires. Ultrasound pulses both power it and send commands, such as monitoring blood pressure, stimulating a nerve or releasing a drug, and a closed-loop version could act on its own.

Adapted into Chinese by Er Mu from “Sound research,” published in Stanford Medicine magazine. Read the original.
